```{r}
#| include: false
options(warn = -1)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(stargazer)
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(modelsummary)
library(quantreg)
library(jsonlite)
library(zoo)
library(sandwich)

temiz_veri <- read_csv("data/analiz_verisi_full.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gelismekte_olan_veri_raw <- read_csv("data/gelismekte_olan_veri.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Exclude countries with fewer than 3 annual observations:
# single-observation units (China 2015, Zambia 2015) contribute zero
# within-country variance to FE estimator and are dropped for cleanliness.
# This reduces the sample from 39 to 37 countries.
obs_counts <- gelismekte_olan_veri_raw %>%
  drop_na(ln_ihracat, ln_reer, ln_gsyh, hukuk) %>%
  count(country)
keep_countries <- obs_counts %>% filter(n >= 3) %>% pull(country)
gelismekte_olan_veri <- gelismekte_olan_veri_raw %>%
  filter(country %in% keep_countries)

temiz_veri <- temiz_veri %>%
  filter(!is.na(reer) & !is.na(ihracat))

analiz_verisi <- temiz_veri %>%
  drop_na(hukuk, regulasyon, reer, ihracat, gsyh) %>%
  mutate(
    ln_ihracat = log(ihracat),
    ln_reer = log(reer),
    ln_gsyh = log(gsyh)
  )

# Panel data structures
p_veri    <- pdata.frame(analiz_verisi,       index = c("country", "year"))
p_veri_em <- pdata.frame(gelismekte_olan_veri, index = c("country", "year"))

# Model estimation
model_politik <- plm(ln_ihracat ~ ln_reer * hukuk + ln_gsyh,
                     data = p_veri, model = "within")
model_em <- plm(ln_ihracat ~ ln_reer * hukuk + ln_gsyh,
                data = p_veri_em, model = "within")
model_em_re <- plm(ln_ihracat ~ ln_reer * hukuk + ln_gsyh,
                   data = p_veri_em, model = "random")

# Driscoll-Kraay robust standard errors
se_scc <- sqrt(diag(vcovSCC(model_em, type = "HC3", maxlag = 4)))

# Pre-computation for inline code
hausman_pre <- phtest(model_em, model_em_re)
t_dk_inter  <- as.numeric(coef(model_em)["ln_reer:hukuk"]) / se_scc["ln_reer:hukuk"]
p_dk_inter  <- round(2 * pnorm(abs(t_dk_inter), lower.tail = FALSE), 3)

sig_note_en <- if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  "Significance levels are reported at the 1 percent, 5 percent, and 10 percent thresholds."
} else {
  "*** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1."
}

```

## Highlights

- Institutional shield null across all estimators and all quantiles once proper inference is applied
- Canay QR positive coefficients vanish under cluster bootstrap — pairs bootstrap systematically understated SEs
- Driscoll-Kraay and GMM confirm null: cross-sectional dependence and dynamic panel bias drove baseline FE significance
- Domestic GDP is the sole robust and dominant determinant of export performance across all specifications
- Sign reversal in first-difference model reveals institutional effects are horizon-dependent, not structurally absent

# Abstract

Does rule of law protect developing-country exporters from exchange rate shocks — or does that protection dissolve once the data are analysed with methods fit for purpose? We address this question using an unbalanced panel of `r nrow(gelismekte_olan_veri %>% tidyr::drop_na(ln_ihracat, ln_reer, ln_gsyh, hukuk))` observations from 37 developing countries over 2000–2022, applying four estimators that each address a distinct, formally confirmed threat to valid inference. Baseline panel fixed effects reproduce the familiar positive interaction between the real effective exchange rate and rule of law — the so-called institutional shield — but the result does not survive. Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, which correct for the strong cross-sectional dependence and serial correlation detected in the data, render the interaction insignificant. Arellano-Bond GMM reaches the same null after eliminating dynamic panel bias. Canay (2011) panel quantile regression with cluster bootstrap standard errors (B = 499, N = 37 clusters) confirms that the interaction is statistically indistinguishable from zero at every point of the export distribution (τ = 0.25, 0.50, 0.75) — earlier reports of significance at lower quantiles turn out to be artefacts of pairs bootstrap, which ignores within-country temporal dependence. A first-difference specification reveals a sign reversal in the short run, but the economic magnitude is negligible (roughly 0.5% of mean annual export variation), pointing to horizon-dependence rather than any structural absence of institutional effects. Throughout, domestic GDP is the only variable that holds up: production scale, not the quality of legal institutions, is the primary engine of export performance in developing economies.

**Keywords:** Export Performance, Real Effective Exchange Rate Volatility, Rule of Law, Panel Quantile Regression, Dynamic Panel GMM, Cross-Sectional Dependence.

**JEL Codes:** F14, F31, C23, C14, O17, O43

# 1. Introduction

Exporting in a developing country is a precarious business. Firms must hedge against currency swings with little access to deep forward markets, navigate customs regimes that shift with political winds, and compete in global markets shaped as much by the global financial cycle as by their own productive capacity. It is natural, then, that a substantial literature has asked whether strong domestic institutions — rule of law, contract enforcement, property rights — can buffer exporters against the worst of these shocks. The idea has intuitive appeal: a country with predictable courts and secure property rights should give exporters the contractual confidence to hedge exposures and sustain long-term trade relationships even when the exchange rate moves against them. This is the *institutional shield* hypothesis (Anderson & Marcouiller, 2002; Arize, Osang & Slottje, 2000; Aman et al., 2024).

The trouble is that the empirical evidence for this shield has almost exclusively been assembled using standard panel fixed-effects models that treat each country as an econometric island — independent of every other. When developing economies are in fact exposed to synchronised shocks (commodity price cycles, financial contagion, the COVID-19 demand collapse), the assumption of cross-sectional independence inflates the apparent precision of coefficient estimates and can make an institutional effect look significant when the underlying signal is a global common factor. Whether the institutional shield survives proper inference correction for global integration is, to our knowledge, an open question.

We answer it directly. Using data from 37 developing countries over 2000–2022, we apply four complementary estimators that address, in turn, the main inference threats the baseline model ignores: Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for cross-sectional dependence and serial correlation; Arellano-Bond Difference GMM for dynamic panel (Nickell) bias; and Canay (2011) panel quantile regression with cluster bootstrap standard errors, which tests whether the shield is operative at different points of the export distribution rather than only on average. The GMM instrument set is restricted to lagged values of the dependent variable to guard against proliferation (Roodman, 2009); REER and institutional quality enter as predetermined regressors. The pattern that emerges from all four approaches is unambiguous: the institutional shield, while positive and significant under naive fixed-effects inference, fails to survive any of the corrections. Across every estimator and every quantile, domestic production scale — real GDP — is the sole robust determinant of export performance. This convergent null is not merely a negative result: it reframes the policy conversation about what developing countries need most to weather exchange-rate shocks.

Section 2 situates the paper in the relevant literature; Section 3 describes the data and empirical design; Section 4 presents the results and diagnostic tests; Section 5 draws policy implications.

# 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework

In the international economics literature, the determinants of export performance are traditionally analysed through the channels of price competitiveness and external demand. The Ricardian trade model developed by Eaton and Kortum (2002) established a structural framework showing how inter-country productivity differences and relative prices shape trade flows. Within the generally accepted analytical framework and the Marshall-Lerner condition, it is argued that an appreciation of the real exchange rate (REER increase) raises the relative prices of exported goods in international markets, weakening external competitiveness and negatively affecting export volume (Aman, Mallick & Nemlioglu, 2021; Bulut & Yaşar, 2023). Particularly in developing economies, exchange rate shocks can lead to significant contractions in trade performance by squeezing the profit margins of exporting firms when the local currency is overvalued (Chamindani, 2019; Khan, Khan & Ahmad, 2024). However, the insufficiency of classical macroeconomic variables alone in explaining export dynamics made it imperative — especially from the 1990s onwards — to integrate the New Institutional Economics perspective into trade models. According to the theoretical framework developed by Douglass North (1990), institutions are the "rules of the game" that structure economic interactions, and economic activities are promoted in environments where property rights and legal predictability are secured, thereby reducing transaction costs. This theoretical foundation is reinforced by the transaction cost theory conceptualised by Coase (1937) and Williamson (1990); indeed, factors such as asymmetric information, opportunism risk, and asset specificity act as "hidden taxes" restricting international trade in environments where the legal infrastructure is weak (Ruzekova, Kittova & Steinhauser, 2020, pp. 146–149). This transformation, as also emphasised by Rodrik (2000), placed institutional infrastructure at the centre of the idea that it is indispensable for high-quality and sustainable economic growth.

Empirical studies examining the direct effect of institutional quality on international trade show that the rule of law, contract enforcement, and bureaucratic efficiency are primary determinants of export volume and diversification. Acemoglu and Robinson (2012) and Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2005) highlighted that institutions are a more dominant engine of growth than factors such as geography and mere openness, indicating that only competitive exchange rate policies would be insufficient to create sustained export growth in countries where property security is weak (Rodrik, Subramanian & Trebbi, 2004). On the structural determinacy of legal and contractual security (contract enforcement) in international trade, Levchenko (2007) and Nunn (2007) demonstrated that countries with well-developed legal institutions gain a clear comparative advantage particularly in goods with high contract intensity and product complexity (Frensch, Horvath & Huber, 2021, pp. 4–6). Indeed, Méon and Sekkat (2004, pp. 1479–1486) econometrically found that bureaucratic inefficiency and weak rule of law directly undermine manufacturing exports and hinder the integration of developing countries into the world economy. In the literature, it is argued that firms operating in countries with high-quality legal institutions are able to manage asymmetric information problems and cross-border transaction risks more effectively thanks to contractual security (Li, Vertinsky & Zhang, 2012).

Firm-level micro evidence supports this macro theory; for example, Mwatu (2022, p. 494) demonstrated that advanced institutional structures directly facilitate firms' entry into and retention in export markets by alleviating financial constraints and bureaucratic barriers. Helpman, Melitz and Rubinstein (2008) proposed a two-stage estimation framework accounting for selection bias in export decisions, pointing out that institutional quality directly affects not only export volume but also the probability of entry into export markets; this finding strengthens the micro-based mechanism explanation of the institutional shield hypothesis. At the macro level, not only the level of institutional quality within the exporting country but also the "institutional distance" between trading partners emerges as a critical parameter. Ezzat and Zaki (2022, pp. 143–156), in gravity model estimations for MENA countries, demonstrated that as the political and institutional quality (rule of law) gap between trade partners increases, the probability of signing deep trade agreements falls significantly; and that increasing the enforceability of agreements directly expands trade volume. Similarly, Abreo, Bustillo and Rodriguez (2021, pp. 4–5) in the Latin American context, and Afonso et al. (2025, pp. 1–23) for both developed and developing countries, empirically confirmed the indisputable role of institutional efficiency on international trade. In this context, institutional development not only increases total trade volume but also enables countries to shift their comparative advantages towards more complex and institutionally intensive goods (Bustaman et al., 2022, p. 9). Tadesse, Shukralla and Fayissa (2019, pp. 4235–4236) further show that institutional infrastructure is a key variable in reducing transaction costs, and that no permanent improvement in bilateral trade costs can be achieved until rule of law surpasses a certain threshold value.

Recent research on the exchange rate–institutional quality interaction, which constitutes the original focus of this study, reveals that institutions serve as a critical "moderator" capable of absorbing or transmitting exchange rate shocks. Anderson and Marcouiller (2002, pp. 342–343) established theoretically and empirically that insecurity — manifested through weak contract enforcement and unpredictable property rights — systematically distorts trade patterns in ways that price-based models cannot capture; bilateral trade contracts for less between country pairs with weak legal institutions, even controlling for income and distance. Their framework implies a non-monotonic relationship between exchange rate volatility and trade: where institutional safeguards are absent, volatility compounds existing contracting hazards and suppresses trade sharply, whereas in institutionally robust environments the same volatility increment is absorbed through contractual hedging and risk-sharing mechanisms. Complementing this theoretical prediction, Arize, Osang and Slottje (2000) provide panel evidence across thirteen developing countries that exchange rate volatility exerts a consistently negative and significant effect on export volumes — an effect that the authors show is more pronounced in countries with shallow financial markets and weaker enforcement capacity. In countries with strong institutional structures and property security, the cost increases created by real exchange rate appreciations can be compensated by the lower risk premium and reduced transaction costs provided by institutional confidence (Aman et al., 2024, pp. 487–490; Baxa & Paulus, 2024, p. 1734). Recent advances in econometric modelling — particularly Non-Linear ARDL (NARDL) approaches — have also revealed the asymmetric nature of the exchange rate–export relationship. Asymmetric panel analyses conducted by Urgessa (2024, p. 18) and Ashour (2023, pp. 16–29) for developing countries confirm that positive exchange rate volatility sharply reduces export earnings, and that risk-averse firms rapidly withdraw from international markets when the institutional shield is weak.

Conversely, in developing economies where the rule of law is weak, institutional deficiencies — combined with exchange rate volatility — deepen risks for exporters and make international trade far more vulnerable to external shocks. Indeed, Aman, Granville, Mallick and Nemlioglu (2024, pp. 486–510) empirically demonstrate that mere trade and financial openness is insufficient on its own to enhance external competitiveness in developing markets, and that high-quality legal institutions are indispensable for REER-driven depreciation to translate into sustained export performance. Abdi and Mohamed (2025, p. 2) similarly emphasise that in environments where institutions are ineffective, high transaction costs emerge and exporters are unable to benefit from the advantage of a depreciating local currency. This demonstrates that strategies focused only on external price advantages (devaluation) are incomplete for developing countries; for sustainable external trade success, structural reforms that strengthen property rights and the legal system serve the strategic function of an "institutional shield" (Baxa & Paulus, 2024, p. 1734; Aman et al., 2021, pp. 399–402).

# 3. Data and Methodology

### 3.1. Data Sources and Variable Definitions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-desc1a
#| tbl-cap: "Table 1a: Descriptive Statistics — Full Sample (2000–2022)"
#| results: asis
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

columns <- c("ln_ihracat", "ln_reer", "ln_gsyh", "hukuk")
labels  <- c("ln(Exports)", "ln(REER)", "ln(GDP)", "Rule of Law")

desc1a <- data.frame(
  "Variable"       = labels,
  "N"              = sapply(columns, function(v) sum(!is.na(analiz_verisi[[v]]))),
  "Mean"           = sapply(columns, function(v) round(mean(analiz_verisi[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), 3)),
  "Std. Dev."      = sapply(columns, function(v) round(sd(analiz_verisi[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), 3)),

  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)

res_kable <- kable(desc1a,
      format = ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "html"),
      align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"),
      escape = FALSE)

if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  res_kable <- res_kable %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
                  full_width = TRUE,
                  position = "center")
}
res_kable
```

The data used in this study consist of an annual panel dataset covering the period 2000–2022. The sample was drawn from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) database (World Bank, 2024a) to capture the relevant data availability and institutional heterogeneity across countries. The dependent variable, export performance, is represented by goods and services exports at constant prices ($ln\_exports$). The key independent variable, the real effective exchange rate ($ln\_reer$), reflects the real value of a country's currency relative to its trading partners.

To represent institutional quality — the original focus of this study — the "Rule of Law" ($rule\_of\_law$) index from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) dataset (World Bank, 2024b) is used. This index scores elements that directly affect property security, including the protection of property rights, judicial independence, and contract enforceability, on a scale from −2.5 (weak) to +2.5 (strong). National real GDP ($ln\_gdp$) is included in the model as a control variable to account for each country's domestic export capacity (scale effect).[^1]

[^1]: World real GDP ($ln\_world\_gdp$) was also tested during the modelling phase to control for external demand shocks and global fluctuations. However, adding this variable — which varies only over time and contains no cross-country variance — to the panel created excessive multicollinearity with time trends and year-specific fixed effects under two-way fixed effects assumptions. The Driscoll-Kraay estimator — which controls for cross-sectional dependence at the core of this study — mathematically dampens global external shocks and time trends by its nature, the $ln\_world\_gdp$ variable was excluded from the final estimation model in order to preserve scientific consistency.

The final sample of 37 developing countries was determined by three sequential criteria: *(i)* World Bank income classification — only non-"High Income" economies are included to maintain institutional and structural comparability; *(ii)* REER data availability — countries lacking a sufficient REER series in the WDI database (including Türkiye, due to structural gaps) are excluded; *(iii)* minimum panel depth — countries with fewer than three complete annual observations across all model variables are dropped, as they cannot generate within-country variance for the fixed effects estimator.

We acknowledge a potential selection concern: countries satisfying criterion *(ii)* tend to be more financially integrated and institutionally developed within the developing-country universe, since REER construction requires bilateral trade weight data typically available only for countries with active IMF reporting relationships. This implies the sample may underrepresent the most institutionally fragile states — precisely where the institutional shield hypothesis would matter most. This limitation is documented explicitly as a boundary on the generalisability of the findings. The complete list of included countries, along with their regional classification and panel coverage, is presented in Table A1 (see Appendix).

Examining Table 1, the average value of the rule of law index in the developing country sample is negative (`r round(mean(gelismekte_olan_veri$hukuk, na.rm=TRUE), 2)`). This indicates that institutional infrastructure elements — such as property rights, contract security, and legal predictability — are structurally weak in the countries included in the analysis. This institutional weakness and environment of uncertainty empirically validates the core motivation of our model investigating the effect of exchange rate shocks on exporters and the function of institutions as a "shield of trust".
